questions.question: Maya has a rectangular library card. It is 12 cm long and 8 cm wide, and it is not a square. If she folds the card so that the two halves land exactly on top of each other, how many different folds like this are possible? In other words, how many lines of symmetry does the rectangle have?
options: 2 lines of symmetry
4 lines of symmetry
1 line of symmetry
0 lines of symmetry
questions.explain: A line of symmetry is a fold line where the two halves match exactly, and a rectangle has only 2: one across the middle the short way and one across the middle the long way. The common trap is answering 4 by counting the two corner-to-corner diagonals — folding a 12 cm by 8 cm rectangle corner to corner makes a long side land on a short side, so the halves do not match.

questions.question: Liam has a rectangular paper flag that is 20 cm long and 10 cm wide. He wants to fold it once so that the two halves cover each other perfectly, with no paper sticking out. Which fold will do this?
options: Fold it from one corner straight across to the opposite corner
Fold it so that the two short 10 cm edges meet
Fold up only the bottom 3 cm strip of the flag
Fold one long 20 cm edge over so it meets a short 10 cm edge
questions.explain: Bringing the two 10 cm edges together folds the flag across the middle of its length, so every point lands on its mirror image and nothing sticks out. The usual trap is the corner-to-corner fold: it makes two triangles of the same size, but a 20 cm side lands on a 10 cm side, so the halves do not match.

questions.question: A square tile on a Vancouver kitchen floor measures 30 cm on every side. All four sides are equal and all four corners are square. How many lines of symmetry does this tile have?
options: 8 lines of symmetry
2 lines of symmetry
4 lines of symmetry
1 line of symmetry
questions.explain: A square folds onto itself 4 ways: across the middle the up-and-down way, across the middle the side-to-side way, and along each of its two corner-to-corner folds, because all its sides are the same length. Answering 2 is the common trap — that is a rectangle's answer, and it forgets that in a square the corner-to-corner folds really do match.

questions.question: Ms. Chan draws a straight line through a shape. What has to be true for that line to be called a line of symmetry?
options: The line has to split the shape into two pieces that cover the same amount of space
The line has to go from one corner of the shape to the opposite corner
The line has to pass through the exact middle point of the shape
When the shape is folded on the line, the two halves must land exactly on top of each other, like a shape and its mirror image
questions.explain: A line of symmetry is a fold line: the half on one side must be the mirror image of the half on the other side and cover it exactly. Same-size pieces are not enough — a rectangle folded corner to corner gives two equal triangles that still do not land on top of each other.

questions.question: An equilateral triangle has three sides that are all the same length. How many lines of symmetry does it have?
options: 3 lines of symmetry
0 lines of symmetry
1 line of symmetry
6 lines of symmetry
questions.explain: Each fold that runs from one corner to the middle of the opposite side makes the two halves match, and there are 3 corners, so there are 3 lines of symmetry. Answering 1 is the trap: it works for a triangle with only two equal sides, but here all three sides are equal, so all three folds work.

questions.question: Printed capital letters can have line symmetry too. Which of these letters has exactly 2 lines of symmetry?
options: A
H
T
Z
questions.explain: The letter that looks like two posts joined by a bar folds onto itself both up-and-down through the middle and side-to-side through the middle, so it has 2 lines of symmetry. The letters shaped like a tent or a table have only the one up-and-down fold, and the zig-zag letter has none, even though it looks the same when turned upside down — turning is not folding.

questions.question: A regular hexagon has 6 sides that are all the same length and 6 equal corners. How many lines of symmetry does it have?
options: 3 lines of symmetry
2 lines of symmetry
6 lines of symmetry
12 lines of symmetry
questions.explain: In a regular shape, the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides, so a regular hexagon has 6: three folds joining opposite corners and three folds joining the middles of opposite sides. Answering 3 is the trap — it counts only the corner-to-corner folds and forgets the side-to-side ones.

questions.question: Which of these shapes has exactly 2 lines of symmetry?
options: A square with 4 sides of 8 cm
A triangle whose three sides are 5 cm, 6 cm and 9 cm
An equilateral triangle with 3 sides of 7 cm
A rectangle that is 12 cm long and 5 cm wide
questions.explain: A rectangle that is not a square folds onto itself in exactly 2 ways: across the middle the long way and across the middle the short way. Watch the trap of picking the square — because all its sides are equal, the corner-to-corner folds also work, giving it 4, while the triangle with three different sides has none.

questions.question: Priya has a rectangular piece of construction paper, 24 cm by 16 cm. She folds it once from one corner straight across to the opposite corner and says, ‘This is a line of symmetry, because now I have two triangles that are exactly the same size.’ What is the best reason Priya is wrong?
options: She is right: the fold passes through the middle of the rectangle, so it is a line of symmetry, as every centre fold is
She is right: the two triangles have the same size, so the fold is a line of symmetry, since equal halves are the test
The two triangles do not land on top of each other — the 24 cm side lands on the 16 cm side, so paper sticks out
She is wrong because a rectangle has no lines of symmetry at all, since its long sides and short sides can never match up
questions.explain: Same size is not the test — the test is whether the two halves land exactly on top of each other when folded, and on a 24 cm by 16 cm rectangle a long side would have to cover a short side, so paper sticks out. A rectangle does have symmetry, but only the 2 folds through the middles of opposite sides.

questions.question: A community garden bed in Kelowna is a rectangle 6 m long and 4 m wide. The gardeners want to lay one straight path that acts as a line of symmetry, so the two halves of the bed are mirror images. Which path works?
options: A path from one corner straight across to the opposite corner, giving two triangles of equal size
A path from the middle of one 4 m side straight across to the middle of the opposite 4 m side
A path from the middle of one 4 m side straight to a corner on the opposite side, because it starts halfway
A path running along one whole 6 m side, from corner to corner, since the longest edge is the mirror line
questions.explain: Joining the middles of the two 4 m ends cuts the bed into two 6 m by 2 m halves that fold exactly onto each other, so it is a line of symmetry. The corner-to-corner path is the classic trap: it makes two equal triangles, but folding on it puts a 6 m side onto a 4 m side, so the halves do not match.

questions.question: Noah designs a rectangular school banner 60 cm wide and 40 cm tall. In the exact centre he prints one large maple leaf, and that leaf has exactly 1 line of symmetry, running straight up and down through its middle. Counting the banner and the printed leaf together as one whole design, how many lines of symmetry does the finished banner have?
options: 2 lines of symmetry
4 lines of symmetry
1 line of symmetry
0 lines of symmetry
questions.explain: A fold only counts if the picture matches too, so the plain rectangle's side-to-side fold is lost — the leaf would land upside down — leaving just the up-and-down fold through the middle, which both the rectangle and the leaf share. Answering 2 is the trap of counting the rectangle's folds and forgetting the design printed on it.

questions.question: Four students in Ms. Dhillon's class each made a claim about lines of symmetry. Which claim is correct?
options: Every shape with 4 sides has 4 lines of symmetry, one for each side
A rectangle has no lines of symmetry, because its sides are not all the same length
A rectangle that is 10 cm by 6 cm has 4 lines of symmetry, because folding corner to corner makes two equal triangles
A square has 4 lines of symmetry, because a fold along either corner-to-corner line still makes the two halves match exactly
questions.explain: In a square all four sides are equal, so the corner-to-corner folds really do make the halves land on top of each other, giving 4 lines of symmetry in total. The trap is copying that idea onto a 10 cm by 6 cm rectangle: there the corner-to-corner fold makes equal triangles but puts a long side on a short side, so a rectangle has only 2.
